# Perdition Gulch

## I.

The thought arrived before she opened her eyes, and it belonged to no one but her.

This was new. Thirty-seven years of thinking had never produced something so solitary, so unwitnessed from the inside, and for a moment Elm held still on the mattress the way a person holds still when she hears a floorboard creak in an empty house. The thought was small — only that the light through the curtain was the color of a tooth — but it sat in her mind without echo, without the familiar sense of it being received even as it was conceived, and the silence where the reception should have been was so total that she put her hand over her mouth as though she had said something obscene.

She did not call out. She turned her head. The other pillow held the shape of nothing. It was cold the way stone is cold, not recently vacated but *uninhabited*, the cotton ticking carrying no warmth, no scent, no indent from a skull that had lain there every night since the two of them were girls sharing a rope bed in their father's house outside Cheyenne. Elm touched the pillow with two fingers.

Nothing.

Not the nothing of sleep, which she had known — the blurred, warm nothing of her sister's dreaming mind, thoughts loose as fish in dark water. This was structural nothing, the nothing of a room from which the furniture has been removed so completely that the floor shows rectangles of darker wood where things once stood.

She sat on the edge of the bed. She put her feet on the floor. The boards were gritty with alkaline dust that came through the walls now no matter how often she swept, a fine white powder that tasted of the creek bed, which had been dry since August. She was forty-three years old. She had brown hair going gray at the temples, hands that were large for a woman, a mole below her left ear that her sister also had, below the right. She had been, until sometime in the night, one-half of something. Now she was one-half of nothing, which is a number that does not exist.

Through the window — warped glass, the pane set crooked in its frame so the world outside bent slightly at the vertical, as though Perdition Gulch were already folding in on itself — she could see the length of Main Street in the early light. A dog, the color of dirt, was tied to the rail outside the land office, lying on its side with its tongue out. It had been tied there since the previous afternoon, and no one had watered it, because the man who ran the land office had gone to Helena three weeks ago and had not come back and had not sent word. The water wagon was making its morning pass, Horace Geld driving, and behind the wheels the dust lifted and hung in the air without settling. There was no wind to settle it and no dew to weight it down. It simply rose and stayed, the way everything in Perdition Gulch now rose and stayed: debts, grievances, the smell of the dead cattle on the Alderson flats south of town, the sound of the well crank at four in the morning as families who used to draw water openly now crept to the well in the dark, filling whatever they had, afraid that drawing in daylight would invite the question of whether there would be enough.

The well was dropping a foot a week. The creek had been dead since August. The springs that fed the horse troughs at the east end of town had slowed to a seep and then to a dark stain and then to nothing, and old Geld's water wagon was making ever-longer runs to the river seven miles north, returning with barrels that were three-quarters full because the river itself was low and the road back rough and the water sloshed out through staves that had shrunk in the heat. The land around the town was the color of old bone. The sagebrush had gone from gray-green to gray to a brittle gray-white that crumbled when you touched it, and the topsoil, which had never been deep, was lifting off the ground in sheets when the wind did blow, which it did twice in September, filling the air with a pale particulate that stung the eyes and coated the horses' nostrils and left a film on the inside of every glass in every building and tasted, when you licked your lips, of nothing. The land was becoming nothing. It was losing capacity. It was forgetting how to hold water, how to anchor dust, how to keep the roots of things gripped in the dark below the surface, and in the losing it was becoming something else — something smooth and blank and unrecognizable, a place that no longer remembered what it had been for.

Elm sat on the edge of the bed and looked at the town through the warped glass and felt the thought still sitting in her mind — *the light is the color of a tooth* — unshared, unreceived, hers alone, and she did not know what to do with it.

She did not yet know that the word for what she was feeling was *freedom*. And she did not yet know that the word for what she had lost was *everything else*.

---

## II.

Three years before the morning of the cold pillow, on a night in October when the creek was still running and the well was full and the smell of the town was woodsmoke and horse and the mineral sweetness of water over shale, a man named Everett Pace rode into Perdition Gulch with four men behind him and a satchel of contracts in his saddlebag and the authority of the Northern Pacific Railroad in his breast pocket and the absolute certainty, born of fourteen successful acquisitions along the Yellowstone corridor, that the nine ranchers south of the creek would sign or be signed for.

He was a surveyor by title and a negotiator by practice and a bully by temperament, and he had been told that Perdition Gulch was a town of perhaps three hundred souls with no sheriff, no telegraph, no newspaper, and no organized resistance, and this was true in every particular and none of the ones that mattered.

Pace and his men stabled their horses at the livery and walked to the Adeline, which was the only saloon and which stood at the south end of Main Street with its doors open to the evening in a way that Pace mistook for welcome. They ordered whiskey. They were loud in the manner of men who wished to be overheard. Pace spread a map on the bar and talked about the rail line in a voice calibrated to carry — the route, the grading, the need for right-of-way through the creek valley, the compensation being offered, the *inadvisability* of declining. His four men, who were not surveyors, who carried revolvers in holsters that had been oiled recently and positioned for speed, did not speak. They did not need to. They leaned against the bar and looked at the room the way you look at something you are measuring for demolition.

The woman sitting at the far end of the bar had been there before they arrived. She was drinking water — she always drank water; alcohol was an interference she could not afford — and she was watching Pace without appearing to, the way a bird watches from a wire: still, tilted, recording. Her name was Fen. She was fifty-one years old. She had a face like the flat of a shovel and hands that were always still and eyes that moved in a way that unsettled people, because they moved too precisely, tracking things that no one else could see, as though she were reading text in the air.

Fen was reading text in the air.

Not literally — she would have said, if asked, that it was more like a library. Everything she had ever perceived was stored, organized, cross-referenced, and retrievable, and the words coming out of Pace's mouth were being checked, in real time, against every document she had ever seen, every conversation she had overheard, every deed and survey and contract and letter and territorial filing that had passed through Perdition Gulch or any of the four towns she had lived in before. She did not forget. She *could not* forget. This was the nature of the thing she carried, the capacity that had no name she was willing to use, and it had made her, over time, into something that was less a person than an archive that happened to breathe.

She waited until Pace paused to drink. Then she said, without raising her voice:

"The right-of-way offer is fourteen cents an acre. You told your principals in Billings it would be twelve. The difference is three hundred and eighty dollars across the nine parcels, which you intend to keep. The contract also includes a clause — section nine, paragraph four, which you did not read aloud — granting the railroad water rights to the creek in perpetuity, which would allow diversion for locomotive supply at the cost of the downstream ranches and this town. You were sent with authority to offer twenty cents. You chose fourteen because you thought no one here could read."

She said this in the same tone a person might use to read a grocery list. She did not look at Pace. She looked at her water glass.

Pace set down his whiskey. His face did something complicated — surprise, fury, recalculation — and then settled into the particular blankness of a man who has been caught and is deciding how to be dangerous about it.

"Who told you that?"

"No one told me anything, Mr. Pace. You wrote it. April sixteenth. Blue ink, on railroad letterhead, to a Mr. Carroll in Billings. You misspelled *perpetuity*."

She picked up her water glass and drank.

Later — much later, well past midnight, after the whiskey had done its work and the four hired men had grown restless in the way armed men grow restless when they sense that their purpose has been understood and preempted — there was the matter of the knife. One of Pace's men, the youngest, had gotten into an argument with a ranch hand named Cole over a card game that may or may not have involved cheating but certainly involved pride, and the argument had produced a blade, and the blade had found the forearm of the man who walked between them.

Doss did not look like a healer. He looked like a farrier who drank, which he also was. He was forty-six years old, thick through the shoulders, with a beard that was going white in patches and hands that were scarred from the work of shoeing horses and the work of other things he did not discuss. He stepped between Cole and the hired man with the unhurried authority of a person who has been struck many times and fears it the way you fear rain — as an inconvenience, not a danger. The knife caught him across the outer forearm, a clean slice that opened the skin in a line six inches long and welled immediately with blood.

Doss looked down at his arm. He wrapped it with a bar rag. He told both men to sit down, which they did, because something in his voice made sitting down seem like the only reasonable response to having been alive for as long as they had been.

He went outside. He stood in the dark for forty-five minutes. Then he came back in.

The saloon had not emptied. Pace was still at the bar, recalculating. The four hired men were still positioned around the room, though their posture had shifted from intimidation to the wary alertness of men who understood that the geography of the situation was not what they had been told. Doss walked to the bar. He unwrapped the rag from his forearm. He held his arm up to the lantern light and rolled his sleeve back slowly, the way you show a card you know will take the hand.

The skin was clean. Not scarred — *clean*. Unbroken. There was dried blood on the rag and on his shirt and on the bar where he'd pressed his arm, but the forearm itself was unmarked, smooth, as though the knife had cut only the idea of him and the idea had declined to be wounded.

The youngest hired man stared at Doss's arm. Then he looked at the rag. Then he looked at the arm again.

"I cut you," he said.

"You did," Doss said.

Doss ordered a whiskey. He drank it with the arm still bared, the skin catching the lamp glow, and he did not explain. He did not need to. The hired man looked at his own knife, then back at the phantom wound, and what passed across his face was not understanding but something older and less manageable: the suspicion that the rules governing flesh might not be uniform, that there were people walking in the world to whom the ordinary consequences did not apply, and that he was possibly standing in a room with one of them.

This was the desired effect. Doss knew it was the desired effect. He had calibrated the moment — the timing, the lighting, the slow unwrapping — with the precision of a man who had done this before, because he had done this before, because the thing he carried was not only the capacity to heal but the knowledge, refined over decades, of how to deploy the evidence of that capacity as a weapon. He did not think of it as intimidation. He thought of it as *economy*.

Outside the saloon — and this detail must be recorded, though no one inside registered it — a child was standing in the dark. He was twelve years old. He was barefoot. He was leaning against the wall next to the door, which was open, and he was listening, but he was not listening with his ears. The thoughts of the men inside reached him the way sound reaches a person underwater: diffuse, pressure-borne, inescapable. He could hear Pace calculating his next move. He could hear the youngest hired man's terror, which tasted, in the child's reception, like iron and bile. He could hear Doss's satisfaction and Fen's cold cataloguing and the ranch hand Cole's drunken shame and, beneath all of it, the low ambient hum of the rest of the bar's occupants, people whose thoughts were smaller, less vivid, but cumulatively loud, a room full of lit candles seen from a distance.

The child — call him Wren, though this was not the name he went by; people in Perdition Gulch called him Boy or Kid or Hey or nothing at all, because a child who appeared from nowhere and seemed to belong to no one resisted the permanence of a name — Wren pressed his back against the wall and closed his eyes and listened to the hired men and then walked, without hurrying, to the rear entrance of the general store, where Elm was stocking shelves by lamplight.

"They're going to burn the Alderson barn tonight," he said. "After the saloon closes. Two of them. The one with the hat band and the one who doesn't talk. They think it'll scare the others into signing by morning."

Elm put down the tin she was holding. She looked at Wren and, simultaneously, she did not look at Wren, because looking, for Elm, was not a unitary act. She saw the boy in front of her and she also saw, through a window half a mile north, the street outside the boarding house where her twin sister was standing on the porch, watching the same darkness, feeling the same information arrive. They did not need to discuss it. The thought moved between them the way blood moves between chambers of a heart — not transmitted, not communicated, but *circulated*, a single awareness housed in two skulls.

By midnight, Elm was at the Alderson barn. Her sister was at the livery, where the hired men's horses were stabled. The two men with the assignment — the one with the hat band and the silent one — found the Alderson property dark, the barn locked, and Elm sitting on the fence rail with a rifle across her knees and an expression that suggested she had been there for hours.
